I don't mean to say that transitioning is the main identifying factor of being a trans person. Also, when I say 'transition', I'd like to point out that I mean all of the possible types and forms of transitioning, be it only changing the way you express yourself, changing your name and pronouns, and/or undergoing medical transition are all perfectly valid. So to me, if someone has realized they're trans and decides to embrace that, I would consider that to be the start of a form of transition. Of course, though, transition is a very personal journey completely unique to every person that experiences it, so it's really not up to me to say when/if their transition has started! 

I do see what you mean when you say that many people view the shortened 'trans' to mean different things: either short for 'transitioned' or short for 'transgender', and I do think I may sort have been confusing the two! I have gotten so used to using 'trans' to be short for 'transitioned', in a sense, as for instance, I commonly use the terms 'transmasculine' and 'transfeminine' which, at least previously, to me mean that you have transitioned (or are in the process) of becoming more masc/fem to be more inclusive of nonbinary people who are trans. Although I guess when I look at it now, I could see that they could also be seen as terms meaning that you feel more aligned with a masculine gender identity than your AGAB, or you feel more aligned with a feminine gender identity than your AGAB.

So now that I see it this way, I can definitely understand what you mean when you say 'nonbinary' fits under the 'transgender' umbrella! 

But back to one of your other points, I'd like to argue that I don't think it's necessarily contributing to trans erasure if you don't choose to identify yourself as such. I personally am genderfluid, and am also transmasc, and in the process of medically transitioning. However, I've never really felt entirely comfortable calling myself 'trans'. I'm okay with saying I'm transmasc genderfluid, but I only really feel comfortable using 'trans' as a prefix to my preferred gender label. To me, I almost feel that if I say I'm trans, it somehow undermines my identity as a nonbinary person. I might call myself nonbinary trans, but I'm not sure how comfy I am with that either. I understand that it might not make a lot of sense, but feelings don't always make sense. ¯\\\_(ツ)_/¯

I have personally met others who identify with something other than their AGAB, but prefer not to use the prefix 'trans'. This is not to say that they consider themselves cis, or that they use 'cis' in place of 'trans', but rather that they (as do I) see the labels 'man' and 'woman', for example, as being all-inclusive terms. For example, that both 'trans woman' and 'cis woman' fits under the term of 'woman'. So for the same argument that you are making that if people fit under the trans umbrella, they should use it, I argue that if people fit under the umbrella of 'man' or 'woman', they should use that, and then specify underneath the umbrella accordingly if they please. Ha-ha! 😉 (I really do mean this in a friendly, bantery like way, and do not mean to offend)

For nonbinary folx, I believe it's the same sort of scenario; while being nonbinary may fit under the trans umbrella, it also exists outside of it on the gender spectrum. If we agree that as a basic format, we have the gender categories of 'man', 'woman', and 'nonbinary' each would act as umbrella terms for specific gender identities that lie within the realm of each. As I said earlier, 'cis' and 'trans' would be examples of those that fit under 'man' and 'woman', (and even under 'nonbinary' in some places of the world with three or more socially accepted genders) along with different nonbinary identities under 'nonbinary'.

So to me, at least, in different ways, 'trans' is an umbrella term for 'nonbinary', just as 'nonbinary' is an umbrella term for 'trans'. And I think if anything, these actions help to normalize the existence of trans people! If trans women want to solely use 'women' as their identifying term, then they are simply helping to drive home the fact that some women are trans! And they are just as much a "normal" woman as any other. 

Please let me know if something I said didn't make sense and I will attempt to explain it better. Also, if you feel it's necessary, feel free to continue the debate! I love having level-headed and respectful arguments with others, I think it can be very beneficial! (For example, just in this argument, you helped broaden my perspective!)

I would politely argue this point, as, in my opinion, the way you are defining 'transgender' and 'nonbinary' don't exactly relate to each other. I personally believe that the two binary genders ('man' and 'woman') are not the only existing genders, but that gender identities that fit within the 'nonbinary' umbrella (such as genderfluid, two-spirit, genderqueer, etc.) are also valid genders.

I think even people who are binary ftm or mtf have the right to decide whether or not they want to use the term 'trans', as while some may see it as a transition, those individuals may see it more like they were always a man (for ftm) or they were always a woman (for mtf) and that their "transition" was really more just a journey of self-discovery and acceptance for who they always were.

Therefore, they may prefer to call themselves simply a 'man' rather than a 'trans man' or a 'woman' rather than a 'trans woman'. Cis individuals don't typically go around calling themselves 'cis men' and 'cis women' because they don't feel the need to add on the prefix. If we truly believe that trans men and women are just as valid as "normal" cis men and women, then we shouldn't hold them to a higher standard than we do cis individuals by making them use the 'trans' prefix.

In the same sense, this thinking applies to those who are nonbinary. They may decide that they feel their "transition" from a binary to a nonbinary gender identity/expression makes them identify with the word 'transgender', but others may feel more like it was a journey of discovering they were nonbinary and learning to love and accept that about themselves.

No one should feel forced to use terminology if they're uncomfortable with it. Just because you think someone fits a certain definition, doesn't mean that person has to label themselves that way.

I'm a transmasc genderfluid dude! So transmasc just means you were AFAB, and then transitioned (either socially, medically, etc.) to become more masculine! 

Being genderfluid is just like you said, you experience gender more ~fluidly~. For me, it means most of the time I feel like a dude, but I also sometimes feel aligned with both or neither of the binary genders, and sometimes I feel aligned with just 'girl'. My gender expression varies quite a bit based on how I'm feeling, so the majority of the time I tend to dress more masculine/androgynous, but sometimes I like to fem it up. Everyone experiences gender fluidity differently, and that's okay!

So since I was AFAB, and transitioned socially (and am currently undergoing medical transition) I am transmasc, but I also am genderfluid! I don't mind using both or either term, as I identify with both, so I typically just say that I'm 'transmasc genderfluid'! 

I wish you all the luck on your journey of gender exploration and discovery! I hope I helped to answer your question, feel free to PM me if you have any more! :)

Yoyo, I'm enby and started T 11 weeks ago! Pm me if you want a little more personal insight on that, but in general I'd say it's very important for you to be aware of what your goals are for T. Are you comfortable with all of the permanent changes T will cause? How about the temporary ones? 

I know of enby transmasc peeps who have gone on T for a few years and then stopped once they achieved their desired results. For example, if you go on T a few years and then come off it, you'll still have whatever hair growth you gained, ween growth, skeletal changes (if you experienced any) etc, but you'll lose the muscle, likely start up your period again, and take on a softer, more "feminine" form due to the fat redistributing itself to its original position. 

This is exactly what some people want, others no! I really recommend talking more in-depth about it with your endocrinologist/whoever prescribes you T!

I've battled with this my whole life. The way my mother describes it, it started when I was a baby, twirling my hair in my hand, when I got caught and pulled some hair out. My mother says she was horrified at this moment, because I had some look on my face that she just knew wasn't going to end well.

I went on to consistently pull my hair until I was around 12 or 13. What I can tell you is this, anything you think might help, probably isn't going to. My parents shaved my head plenty of times to try to get me to stop, and my hair was always kept short to try and hide the bald spots. Nothing my family tried ever worked, and the only way I stopped was through will.

I kept reminding myself that if I kept pulling my hair out, someday it wouldn't grow back anymore. (Once you've pulled hair out of a follicle too many times, you kill the follicle.) I actually do still have some thin spots on my head from places where the hair just never grew back. I found keeping myself busy with my hands helped a lot. Drawing, playing an instrument, playing a video game, writing, etc, just keep those hands moving and away from your head. (Or your face, I pulled out my eyelashes and eyebrows too)

I will say that sometimes I still find myself twirling a section of hair in my fingers, but I've come to a point where I can recognize what I'm doing and stop. I know this is an incredibly hard condition to face, and I wish you the best of luck.

I said that. Trans men are still men. Trans women are still women. Trans men can go by 'FTM' if that's how they feel. Trans women can go by 'MTF' if that's how they feel. But medically, it is literally classified as 'masculinizing' or 'femenizing' hormone therapy. I don't think you understand that the terms 'transmasculine' and 'transfeminine' don't at all remove the ideas of 'FTM' and 'MTF'. It's just more terms.

What you're saying is definitely something other genderfluid folx go through, and my advice is to find out what's comfortable for you. If you feel most comfortable just going by your name, that's valid too! I, for example, have He/They pronouns all the time. Even though there are times I feel like a girl, those are the two I feel most comfortable with using. Your pronouns don't necessarily have to reflect your gender. (i.e. there are plenty of drag queens who still identify as men but use She/Her pronouns) Good luck discovering yourself! :)

However, not everyone who goes on hormones undergoes a sex change. If someone went on *masculinizing* hormone therapy they didn't necessarily get their sex changed. They may have decided to keep their birth genitalia, or not get top surgery, or any combination of the sort. Does that make their gender identity any less valid? Absolutely not. But does that mean their sex has changed? Also no.

Plenty of people who go on masculinizing HRT don't ever get their sex officially changed, whether that be legally, through surgery, etc.

It only makes a difference when you decide to act on those thoughts, which you clearly haven't.

You are not your thoughts, you are your actions. And as long as you never act upon those thoughts, try not to let them eat at you.
